- If sentiment is consistently negative or low (e.g., < 0.3) over recent days, reduce forecast slope or shift mean downward to avoid over-optimism.  
- If model shows steady upward trend with no recent dip, check for overshoot after a spike — cap forecast rise if sentiment turns negative or shows divergence.  
- When true outcome shows sharp drop after a peak, model often overcorrects — adjust forecast to allow for mean reversion, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative.  
- If sentiment is rising (e.g., > 0.7) and model is flat or rising slowly, consider accelerating upward trend slightly — but cap at 1–2% per day if sentiment is volatile.  
- If model forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong downward movement, consider lagged correction — adjust forecast 1–2 days ahead to reflect sentiment shift.  
- Avoid overfitting to recent history — if last 3–5 days show strong volatility, don’t assume trend will continue; use sentiment to guide smoothing or reversal triggers.  
- If sentiment is high but true outcome is low, consider “sentiment gap” — reduce forecast by 1–3% per day if sentiment > 0.8 and outcome < 85% of recent mean.  
- For 30-day horizon, if model is consistently above 85% of recent 10-day average, consider downward bias — adjust if sentiment is weak or negative.  
- If sentiment is rising sharply and model is flat, consider “sentiment momentum” — increase forecast slope by 0.5–1.5% per day if sentiment > 0.75 and rising.  
- If true outcome is below 80% of recent 10-day average, model often overestimates — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day if sentiment is neutral or negative.
